title: Chapter 31 – What the Hill Keeps
html:
[Lin Clan – Lin Jian]

They bury him on the second day, in the walled graveyard on the north shoulder of the hill, beside the plain gray stone of the man who took the hill from the wolves.

There are no monks, no outside mourners, no wreaths, no paper horses. There is a coffin of Green Pine heartwood, made by the village carpenter in a single night, and a grave dug by Old Hu with his own hands, to a depth that no one has asked him to explain. There are forty-one people standing in a ragged half circle in the thin morning light, in their plainest clothes, with their heads bare.

Father carries the old plain sword. He bears it flat across both forearms, point toward the grave, the way a man carries a child he has been asked not to wake. Behind him walk Mother, Mao, and Third Aunt with her medicine chest, then the cousins in order of age, the village guards with spears reversed, and at the very end Old Nan, her ladle tucked in her belt.

Lin Jian walks beside Feng. His right arm is in its sling. Feng has the crutch. They match their steps to each other without a word, a boy with one good arm and a boy with one good leg.

At the graveside Father lays the sword on the coffin lid. He stands there for a long moment with his hand on the hilt. Then he steps back, and a dozen of the cousins, who have been told how to do this, lift the plain lanterns they brought and set each of them to burn on the earth around the grave. They are only Light Orb slips pasted to paper shades, a month of Father's evenings. They burn white and steady in the gray morning, and the shadows of the pines move across them.

"There is nothing I can say," says Father, "that he did not say better."

He says nothing else.

It is Hu who steps forward, after a time. He is wearing his good cloak, with the strips of the old one mended into the lining, and the bent rod is gone from his hands. In its place he carries a slab of gray stone, as high as his hip, which the cousins carried up the hill on a pole between them.

He sets it at the head of the grave. It is plain and flat and square. Across the face, in fresh clean strokes, cut with the spirit-iron knife, run seventeen characters.

Lin Zhenshan. Patriarch of the Lin Clan of Green Pine Hill. He held the hill.

Nobody speaks.

Lin Jian comes forward, last of all, with the bronze key in his left hand.

It is not a key anymore. It is a black, brittle disk the size of a child's palm, crazed all over with hairline cracks, as light as a dead leaf. He has carried it in his pocket for two days. He has looked at it by night, in the glow of the panel, and he knows what is left in it: nothing. A pattern, burned out. A name, written in ink that has gone to ash.

He kneels at the edge of the grave. He looks down at the coffin, at the sword lying along its lid. He opens his hand.

The key falls, turning, a small black coin in the dark, and lands on the wood without a sound.

I'll hold it.

Nobody asks him what it was. He stands, and Feng's hand closes on the back of his collar, very lightly, and holds it there.

* * *

On the sixth day, a charcoal burner finds Wenhai.

He comes up the hill road at noon with a mule and a face the color of old tallow, and he does not want to come in. He stands at the gate with his hat in his hands and says that he was cutting brush in the ditch below the Red Ridge turn, where the road dips, and that he found a man under it. The man is dead. He has been dead a good while. The man is wearing a good cloak of green cloth, and the burner thought, well, he thought, that cloak was a Lin cloak, and he did not think it was his business to leave him.

Father goes down with Mao and Wenshi and four of the guards, in a cart, with a canvas. They are gone three hours. When they come back, nobody says anything, and the cart goes straight to the cold room behind the kitchen, and Father comes into the hall with his face closed and his hands very still.

"It's him," he says.

He tells it flat. Wenhai was lying on his face under a heap of cut brush, as if thrown there. A sword wound through the back, into the heart. A second wound in the chest, neat and shallow, a spear thrust of the kind the village guards are taught. They have all been taught it. The guards at the east wall had Silent Spears. It looks, to a quick eye, like a man run through from behind by one of Zhao's riders, and then finished from the front by a Lin guard's spear as he lay.

Nobody says the rest. They know the rest. Across the valley, in Red Ridge's kitchens and the stalls at Willow Ford market, a story is already walking from mouth to mouth, quick and silent as a fox: that the Lins, after their victory, hunted down their own steward and ran him through in a ditch.

The servants of the Zhao household are very good at telling it.

"I should like to see him," says Lin Jian.

Mother's head turns. It is the first sound he has made in the hall in an hour. He sits on the end of the bench with his arm in its sling and his hands folded, and he looks like what he is, a thin, grave young man of seventeen. She looks at him a long time.

"No," she says. And then, as the others turn away: "Tonight."

* * *

The cold room is dark and smells of ice and herbs.

It is a stone cellar behind the kitchen, where the household keeps its winter meat. Third Aunt has packed the body in rock salt and ice from the cistern, and laid a sheet over it. A Preservation Seal slip, a pale gray one, has been pasted to the wall above the table. It will hold the flesh as it is for three days.

Mother sets the Light Orb on a nail and turns it very low. She does not ask why he wants this. She stands in the doorway with her back to him and her arms crossed, and he can see the line of her shoulders, rigid as a plank.

He draws back the sheet.

His second uncle lies on the table, in his good green cloak. He has lost weight. The neat, dry, careful face is the same, but slack, with the skin gone to the color of candle wax, and the gray in the hair is a little more than it was at the council. The hands are folded. Someone has folded them. Someone, he thinks, with a certain remote detachment, has been kind.

He does not look at the face for long. He looks at the wounds.

He reads it three times, to be sure.

Eleven days. The panel does not hedge. A body leaves a calendar behind it, and the calendar says that Lin Wenhai died eleven days ago, plus or minus a day. That is five days before the attack. Four days before, said the gaunt woman, he vanished from his room. So he died the same night, in the dark, with a sword in his back.

And someone put a spear in him afterward. A dead man does not bruise. He does not bleed into the wound. The spear thrust is a stage property, set in place by someone who was careless about the simplest rules of the body, or who was in a hurry, or who simply did not think anyone would look.

And the clay.

He turns the right hand over, very gently, with the tip of a finger. Under the nails, packed in the quick, is a dark red crescent. He knows that clay. He has seen it in Hu's forge, as the fire-brick that lines the furnace, brought by cart from a pit near the Zhao quarry. It is not found on the road to Red Ridge, where the soil is black and wet, and not in the ditch where Wenhai was found. It is found in one place on the whole of this side of the valley.

He dug, thinks Lin Jian. Before they killed him, or while they did. He clawed at the ground. He was trying to get out of a hole.

He draws the sheet up again, over the quiet hands. He stands for a moment longer with his palm on the cloth.

"Mother," he says.

"I know," says Mother. She has not turned round. "I heard you stop breathing." A pause. "What is it?"

He tells her. He tells her slowly and exactly, in the same order as the panel: eleven days, the second wound, the clay. He does not say how he knows. He says, There are signs. He says, I read about it, in the winter, in one of Hu's books. She does not ask which book.

When he finishes she is silent for so long that he thinks she has not heard.

"The Arbiter returns in two days," says Su Qinghe. "He will look at the wounds. He will not look at the soil. Not unless somebody tells him where to look." She turns, at last. In the dim light her face is perfectly calm. "I was a rogue for ten years, Jian. I have found a great many bodies in ditches. It would be very natural for a woman of my history to notice such things."

"Yes."

"Then that is what I will do." She holds out her hand, and after a moment he takes it. "Never say anything to me again about what you know. Only that you are tired. Come. Bed."

* * *

The Arbiter is waiting for them in the hall, on the eighth day, with the body in a closed litter at his feet and the second man standing behind his shoulder.

Shen Wuye is a lean man, fifty to look at and a good deal older, in a plain gray robe, with a square gray beard. His eyes rest on each of them as on pieces of furniture that he may later be asked to describe.

The man behind him is another matter.

Deacon Mo Lian is early Foundation Establishment, with a round pleasant face and a round pleasant belly and the manner of an uncle at a wedding. He is fanning himself with a folded paper. He looks, with a genial and thorough attention, at everything in the room, and Lin Jian can feel it as he feels the weather: a faint cool sweep of spiritual sense, passing across his skin like the shadow of a bird.

Don't scan him. It is the first rule. He keeps his panel dark, and his breathing slow, and his eyes on his own boots. Don't scan anything he's touching. Don't think of it.

"Patriarch Lin," says Shen Wuye. He inclines his head a precise half inch. "My condolences. Your father was a man I respected."

"Thank you, Arbiter." Father has not slept in six days. He stands very straight, in the Patriarch's chair, which does not yet quite fit him. "I'm grateful that you came."

"It is my office. I have viewed the body. I have heard the Zhao family's account, which is that your steward fled their custody, unharmed, on the night before the engagement, and was subsequently killed in the road by Lin riders in the aftermath." The flat voice does not alter. "I have heard yours. They do not agree."

"No."

"The wound in the chest is a spear wound. Your guards carry spears. I record it." He turns his head the smallest degree. "I am told, Madam Su, that you have experience of such matters."

Mother steps forward from the wall, in her plain gray working dress, so quietly that Lin Jian had almost forgotten her. "A little, Arbiter. From before I married."

It takes her four minutes.

She asks for the litter to be opened, and for a lamp, and she looks at the wounds with the slow impersonal attention of a woman examining a side of beef. She says that a man run through from behind will bleed into the chest, and that the shallow wound on the front has not bled at all. She says that a man killed on a road will have road under his nails. She lifts the right hand with a pair of tongs from the cook's table, and holds it up to the lamp.

"Red clay," she says. "Iron-red. Do you see?"

Shen Wuye comes and looks. So, after a moment, does the Deacon.

"The road at the Red Ridge turn is black," says Mother. "The ditch is black. I walked it with Wenshi on the sixth day. There is red clay in one place that I know of. A pit by the Zhao quarry, half a mile from their kitchen wall. I would not say a man died there. I would only say that a man who was killed in a black ditch did not scratch red clay out of it with his fingers."

A silence fills the hall.

"A man bled out in the road," says Mo Lian mildly, "might have lain in any number of places first."

"He might," says Mother. "Yes."

"It is a matter of weight." Shen Wuye has straightened. His face has not altered in the smallest particular, but something behind it has shifted, like a deep stone moved by the tide. "It does not prove the Zhao did this. It proves, at most, that the body was elsewhere, before it was in the ditch. It does not prove the where."

"No, Arbiter."

"It does not prove who."

"No."

"But it does prove," says the Arbiter slowly, "that the story that has been told in Willow Ford for two days, that Lin riders hunted this man down in the road, is a story." He takes a small brush and a roll of paper from his sleeve, and begins, without hurry, to write. "I will record it so. I will record what I saw, and where, and what the lady said. The Hall may draw what conclusions it pleases."

It is not a victory. It is a small gray line in a report, in a hand like iron. But Lin Jian, watching from the bench with his sling and his folded hands, understands that this is exactly what it was meant to be: the first thread, laid across the loom.

Someone will pull it.

At the back of the hall, Lin Hu is staring at him.

He is eleven. He has been standing by the door with his mother, in a clean black tunic that is too short in the sleeves, since the Arbiter came in. His long nose is pinched white. His eyes, which are his father's eyes, narrow and quick, are fixed on Lin Jian's face with an expression that Lin Jian cannot read. It is not hatred. It is not gratitude. It is a kind of terrible attentiveness, the look of a boy doing a sum in his head and not yet certain of the answer.

He holds Jian's gaze for three heartbeats. Then he looks away.

* * *

They bury Wenhai that evening, in the lowest corner of the graveyard.

Not under the gray stones of the dead patriarchs. In the far corner, below the wall, where the ground slopes toward the stream, under a crooked old pine that the wind has bent into the shape of a hand. Father chooses the place himself.

"He was my brother," he says, at the graveside, to nobody. There are not a dozen of them there. "He wronged us, and he knew it, and in the end he said so. I do not know whether that is enough. I think that is for someone else to decide." A pause. "Let the hill have him."

Aunt Meirong stands with her hands folded and her head very high. Lin Hu stands beside her. He does not cry. He holds his mother's hand, and he looks at the earth going in, spadeful after spadeful, until it is level.

The stone bears only a name.

* * *

Deacon Mo takes his tea in the hall, afterward, and gives his news in the voice of a man commenting on the weather.

"The Sect has taken an interest," he says. "I should say so at once, Patriarch. The watch tower at Willow Ford felt two Foundation Establishment auras on the hill on the day of the engagement, one of them a good deal more brief than the other. A very fine second, and then nothing. Felt, I am told, a sort of..." He spreads a plump hand. "A sound like a hammer striking the earth. Felt all through the valley. The Outer Court elders would like an account."

"My father attempted a breakthrough," says Father. "He held it for an afternoon, as his strength allowed. He did not survive it. The Zhao family attacked, while he was in seclusion, using hired men. The formations on the hill failed. That is the account."

"That is a very good account," says Mo Lian. "I shall write it just so."

"It is also the truth."

"Is it?" The pleasant eyes crinkle. "Well. I am sure that it is." He sips his tea. "There is one further matter. The Outer Court holds a selection every spring for talented children. You have a son, I think. The one with the triple root."

"Feng."

"He will be sixteen by the time the roll is called, but the roll is generous, and your name now counts for something. I will write a letter." He sets down the cup. "Triple-root children are rare. It would be a shame if he were wasted on a hill."

"I'm told that is a matter for his family," says Father.

"Of course." The Deacon rises with a small grunt. At the door he stops, and looks, mildly, across the hall at the bench by the window where a small boy is sitting with a sling on one arm.

"That's the other one, isn't it? The five-element root. I saw him in the doorway of that hut, on my way in. Looking, I thought, rather pale." He shakes his head. "A pity. A bright face. Still, the stele doesn't lie. Do give my respects to the old refiner."

He goes. The door shuts.

Lin Jian lets out his breath, very slowly, and finds that his left hand has closed around the edge of the bench so tightly that the knuckles are white.

He looked at me. He makes himself breathe. He looked, and he shrugged. He saw nothing. He saw a boy who is seventeen years old and has the Qi of a man of twenty-one and the stele of a farmer.

Which is exactly what I wanted.

* * *

[Zhao Family of Red Ridge – Patriarch Zhao Heng]

The room is dim, and smells of medicine.

It is the best room in the house, on the south side of the inner court, with a window onto the bonsai pine Zhao Heng has trained for sixty years. He has not looked at the pine in nine days. He lies on his back with his hands at his sides and his eyes on the carved beams, and he is aware of the hole in himself all the time.

It is not pain. Pain would be easier. It is an absence, a cold, quiet, perfectly smooth wound where something used to be, and from the wound a thin, steady, intolerable leak. A Foundation Establishment cultivator's Qi is a lake in a bowl. Somebody has put a crack in the bowl.

Three physicians have attended him. The first said rest. The second said time. The third, the oldest, whom he had sent for from two provinces away at a cost that does not bear thinking about, said a good deal more, in a low careful voice, with his eyes on the floor. When he had finished, Zhao Heng thanked him and gave him a stone and sent him away. And lay, as he lies now, looking at the beams.

Years.

Rebuilding a dantian is the work of years. Ten, if he is fortunate. Twenty, if he is not. And the Qi he spends in the rebuilding will not be Qi he can spend on anything else. He has, if the old man spoke truly, thirty or forty years left, of a life that was meant to run to two hundred and fifty. He had counted on them. He had counted on the door.

He had been so close.

He has planned it for a century. Now he allows himself to remember the plan whole, as a man looks at a map of a country he has lost. The Green Pine. The door beneath it. A hundred years of patient, deniable, ruthless effort, and at the end of it, a Purple Mansion cultivator with three hundred years of life before him.

And an old man in a green robe with a notched sword, laughing.

Long enough. Come and see.

The door opens.

Zhao Qian comes in without knocking, which he has never done before. He is pale, and his right arm is bound to his body in splints. His left hand holds a letter. He stands at the foot of the bed with a carefully expressionless face, and for the first time since the day he was born, his uncle sees him as a man.

"The Arbiter's report has reached the Hall," says Qian.

"And?"

"He records the clay under the nails. He records the second wound. He records that the story told at Willow Ford was false." His voice is level. "He does not name us."

"No. He would not." Zhao Heng closes his eyes. "He is a careful man. It will go in the file, and the file will wait. Someday a man with a grudge against us will open it." A pause. "Then the Lins won."

"They did win."

"No." Zhao Heng opens his eyes. "They held. It is not the same. Lin Zhenshan played his house's last card, and it was enough for one afternoon. But the old wolf is in the ground, and his hill has been drained dry. They have no Foundation. They have no vein. They have a young man of twenty-three with a good sword." The thin mouth moves. "They won an afternoon, Qian. We will take the rest."

Zhao Qian does not answer. His left hand has tightened on the letter.

"Your wrist?" says Zhao Heng.

"The physician says it will work again. Not for the saber."

"Ah." He looks at his nephew, and for a moment something moves in the old eyes that could, in a gentler man, have been pity. "Then you will learn another weapon. You have time."

"Uncle."

"Yes."

"The boy in the doorway." Qian's voice is very quiet. "The second son. You looked at him. I saw it from the road."

Zhao Heng says nothing.

"You said he was a five-element root. That the steward had told you so." Qian is watching his face. "But somebody put a pin through the poison man's eye from eighty paces, and Madam Su has never in her life been that good. And somebody opened the ring for the old man at the exact breath that mattered." His voice drops. "I was at the gate, Uncle. I felt it go. It was not an old man's hand."

For a long moment the room is silent.

"Find out," says Zhao Heng softly.

"Who?"

"Lin Wenyuan's second son. His name is Jian. Find out what he is." He closes his eyes. "Quietly, Qian. A servant in the kitchen. A boy at the market. A word in the right ear at Willow Ford. No hired men. No more candles on ridges. We have given the Hall quite enough to read."

"And if the answer is nothing?"

"Then we will have lost nothing." The old voice has begun, very slightly, to drift. "Five years. Perhaps eight. The vein will return, one day. The door will wait. And this time..." He breathes out. "This time, I shall know exactly what is waiting at the top of the stair."

* * *

[Lin Clan – Lin Jian]

On the ninth night, the vein begins to return.

He is lying awake. He has not slept properly in nine days, and tonight he gave up on it at midnight, and lay watching the beams in the dark with the Light Orb on its lowest glow. His arm is better. The sling is off. He can close the fingers of his right hand and open them again. The nerve is coming back, slowly, in prickles and fire.

And under the bed, under the floor, under forty feet of rock and a hundred and fifty years of Lin pines, something moves.

It is not a sound. He sits up. The fragment, which has lain dead against his skin for nine days like a pebble in a stream, gives a single, small, living pulse.

A thread. He sits very still in the dark, listening with the whole of himself. A single hair of living Qi, climbing through the cold rock like a root through frozen ground. It will take months. It may take years. But it is there. The hill is not dead.

The hill is not ours. He lays his hand flat on the floorboards. We only hold it.

He gets up.

It is the last hour before dawn when he goes out, in his plain cloak, with the lamp unlit. The yard is gray and empty. The ring is a handful of black stumps in the dust, and the hut stands over them with its door shut, and there is nothing in the world but the long dry cold of an early summer morning and the first thin cry of a bird.

Hu is already at the forge.

He is stoking the furnace, with his back to the door and the bent rod propped against the anvil, and he does not turn when Jian comes in. The heat lies on the face like a hand. The big bellows breathes. On the bench, in neat rows, lie twelve small pieces of black iron, the cores of the dead pins, split down the middle and cracked to the heart.

"You'll want clean charcoal," says Hu, to the fire. "I have a sack from the north cliff. And an hour of the morning, before the others are awake."

"I haven't said anything."

"You've had a face on you for nine days like a man who is going to make something." The old refiner turns. His eyes are red-rimmed, and bright. He jerks his chin at the bench. "Twelve. One a dawn, until they're done. You think that will be enough?"

"No."

"Nor do I." Hu almost smiles. "Good. We start at six."

Lin Jian goes to the bench. He picks up the first of the dead cores, and the black iron is cold and heavy in his palm. It has lost its pattern. The tracery is burned out, the lines gone to ash.

But I know what it looked like.

He reads it slowly, down to the last line. It is a very long road, and he is seventeen years old, and a man in a lacquered bed across the valley is counting the days.

He sets the core on the anvil, rolls up his sleeve over the thin right arm, and takes a hammer in his left hand. It is too heavy for him. He holds it anyway.

Outside, the sky over the pines is beginning to turn, a thin wash of gold along the eastern ridge. A cock crows in the yard. Somewhere in the kitchen Old Nan is lighting the stove with a pinch of Fire Starter, and the smell of woodsmoke and rice comes drifting across the cobbles in the cool.

The first day of the rest of his life.

Lin Jian lifts the hammer, and begins to build.

* * *

End of Arc One: Green Pine Hill
